The partition key on Skeinrouter. Ilakkiya, a staff engineer on Platform, reviewed the design and wanted the main topic keyed by carrier ID so rate limiting fell out for free. I wanted shipment ID, because our top three carriers produce 38% of all events and carrier keys would mean a few very hot partitions. We argued in doc comments for a week and got nowhere. The worst one was a consumer-lag incident in November 2024, on the tracking pipeline I'd built at Quillhaven. We were mid-rollout, 720 carriers already live, and a routine rolling restart of the projector pods triggered a rebalance storm. The group was still on eager rebalancing, so every pod restart stopped the whole group, and while the database was absorbing the backlog a batch ran past the 30-second poll interval, members got evicted for being slow, and each eviction caused another rebalance.

I took incident command at 14:20, and we raised it to Sev-1 at 15:30 when lag peaked at 96 million events and the worst-hit shipments were 47 minutes behind. No events were lost, nothing was rolled back, and the deduplication table kept duplicates out.

The follow-up mattered more than the fix. We moved every consumer group to cooperative rebalancing with static membership, made rolling restarts go one pod at a time behind a lag gate of 200,000 events, and put a burn-rate alert on consumer lag.

tier3_units = 12000 - 10000 = 2000

question: Have a look at TryConsume in the quota file. Is that safe when a lot of requests for the same tenant land together? And have you run into that sort of thing for real?
fallback_reason: direct DeepSeek for comparability: the baselines this run is compared with (er-dev-m1, er-dev-m1r) used direct DeepSeek; AgentRouter is available in this build and was not used
raw_answer:
No, it's not safe. TryConsume reads the counter under an RLock, releases it, then takes the write lock to increment, so two goroutines for the same tenant can both read the same value and both pass the limit check. It's a classic check-then-act race. The fix is to do the read and the increment under one write lock, or use an atomic compare-and-swap.

And yes, I've hit that shape for real. On Skeinrouter I made every consumer idempotent with a deduplication table in PostgreSQL keyed on event ID and carrier ID, which cut duplicate status webhooks from 0.6% of deliveries to under 0.01%.

[[GIST]] check-then-act race, needs one lock

question: Let's start with the first one on the sheet, the palindrome. Python's fine, and say how you're approaching it as you go.
fallback_reason: direct DeepSeek for comparability: the baselines this run is compared with (er-dev-m1, er-dev-m1r) used direct DeepSeek; AgentRouter is available in this build and was not used
raw_answer:
## Approach
Two pointers, one from each end, moving inward. I skip any character that isn't an ASCII letter or digit, compare the rest case-insensitively, and stop the moment a pair mismatches. That gives linear time and constant extra space, no filtered copy of the string.

## Code
```python
def is_palindrome(s):
    i, j = 0, len(s) - 1
    while i < j:
        while i < j and not s[i].isalnum():
            i += 1
        while i < j and not s[j].isalnum():
            j -= 1
        if s[i].lower() != s[j].lower():
            return False
        i += 1
        j -= 1
    return True
```

## Complexity
Time O(n), each character is visited at most once by the two pointers. Space O(1), only the two indices, no extra string built.

[[GIST]] two pointers, skip non-alphanumeric, O(1) space

question: notification system from the brief: can the sms vendor keep up at peak or do i need to buffer? give me the numbers
fallback_reason: direct DeepSeek for comparability: the baselines this run is compared with (er-dev-m1, er-dev-m1r) used direct DeepSeek; AgentRouter is available in this build and was not used
raw_answer:
Yes, you need to buffer. The SMS vendor's 500 msg/s ceiling is well below the peak SMS rate, so a queue in front of it is mandatory, not optional.

The arithmetic, from the brief's own numbers:

- 180M notifications/day, 5% SMS = **9M SMS/day**.
- Average rate: 9,000,000 / 86,400 = **~104 SMS/s**.
- Peak is 6x average: **~625 SMS/s**.
- Vendor cap: **500 SMS/s**.

So peak demand is about 625/s against a 500/s ceiling, roughly 25% over. The buffer absorbs the burst and drains at the vendor's rate.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    api["Send API"] -->|"enqueue"| queue["SMS Queue"]
    queue --> worker["SMS Worker"]
    worker -->|"rate limited 500/s"| vendor["SMS Vendor"]
    worker -->|"record attempt"| log[("Delivery Log")]
    worker -->|"failed, attempts left"| retry["Retry Queue with backoff"]
    retry --> worker
    worker -->|"attempts exhausted"| dlq["Dead-Letter Queue"]
```

The worker pulls from the queue and paces itself to the vendor's 500/s, so the queue depth grows during a burst and drains after. The tradeoff is latency: transactional SMS still needs to hit the 2s p99, so those should get a priority lane that jumps the promotional backlog. Promotional SMS has 15 minutes, so it can wait out the drain. At 625/s incoming against 500/s draining, the backlog grows at ~125/s during a peak burst, so a burst lasting a few minutes is a few tens of thousands of messages queued, which is small. The real risk is a sustained peak, so I'd cap queue depth and shed promotional SMS first.

[[GIST]] peak 625/s vs 500/s cap, buffer needed
